To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the obesity paradox is gender-specific and is not seen in patients who have normal serum creatinine levels.
the association between BMI and OS is driven by males and is not observed in patients with low serum creatinine.

1) in the real world, an obesity paradox was seen in melanoma patients receiving PD-1 blockade, with a survival advantage seen in overweight/obese (BMI 25- <35 kg/m²) males; 2) this survival advantage was not seen in females or those with low serum creatinine; 3) the obesity paradox was seen for both PD-1 monotherapy and combination therapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the relationship of BMI with survival and explores gender-based interactions with surrogate markers of body mass composition/malnutrition, in the context of anti-PD- 1 blockade as monotherap or in combination with CTLA-4 blockade.
the relationship between body mass index, serum creatinine levels and gender on survival in melanoma.
the relationship between body composition and survival in the context of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the obesity paradox in advanced melanoma is not a universal phenomenon, but is restricted to a specific subset of patients, predominantly male and obese, who are more likely to have sarcopenic obesity.
the association between BMI and OS is complex and is likely driven by a combination of factors including gender, sarcopenia, malnutrition and other factors.
the association between BMI and improved survival in advanced melanoma patients treated PD-1 blockade is complex and is dependent on gender, serum creatinine and other surrogates of malnutrition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BMI may not be the best predictor of survival in melanma patients treated with PD1-blockade (monotherapy/comb).
the “obesity paradox”, if it exists, is a male gender driven phenomenon in the setting of PD-1 checkpoint inhibition.
“the obesity paradox is not the same as the sarcopenia paradox”.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the “obesity paradox”, which is a well-known phenomenon in the general population, may be present in the context of anti-PD1 therapy in melanoma patients, and that this association is predominantly seen in males with higher creatinine levels, suggesting a potential role for sarcopenia or direct measures of muscle mass as predictors of survival.
the “obesity paradox”, which was previously shown in melanoma patients in the context of monotherapy, is also seen in the context of combination therapy.
obesity is not necessarily protective in all patients with advanced melanoma.
